promptHtml: msum16's worst path starts at x_reg[12][2], a flip-flop of the samples, ends at y_reg[17], and passes through 14 cells of logic between them. Put in order what the data passes through.
explanationHtml: A path starts at a flip-flop's clock and ends at a flip-flop's D. In between, each addition takes its LUTs first, which feed the carry chain's inputs (lesson 6.2), then its CARRY4s, and the next addition takes that sum in. The tempting slip is CARRY4s before LUTs: the LUTs work out what the carry chain adds.
steps: The clock edge reaches x_reg[12][2], and its Q changes.
A LUT3, then a LUT4, take bits of the samples.
Three CARRY4s add them, four bits at a time.
More LUTs and CARRY4s add the sums so far.
The sum reaches y_reg[17]'s D input.

promptHtml: msum32's timing summary says its timing constraints are not met: its worst path arrives 0.5 ns too late for the board's 100 MHz clock. What does that tell you?
explanationHtml: A missed constraint is not an error: Vivado still places and routes the design and writes a bitstream, as it did for msum32. On the board, a flip-flop at the end of a late path can take a wrong value, so the sums may come out wrong. The clock is the board's, which a constraint only describes (lesson 7.2), and a simulation knows nothing of the delays, so msum32's testbench passes.
options: Vivado finished the build and wrote a bitstream; on the board, the sums may come out wrong.
Vivado stopped before writing a bitstream, because a path fails.
Vivado slowed the clock down until every path fits.
The testbench of msum32 fails too, on the same paths.
